newsitem.title: JAPAN: Protesters jeer as British N-ship arrives in Japan.
newsitem.headline: Protesters jeer as British N-ship arrives in Japan.

text.p: Jeered by anti-nuclear protesters, a British ship carrying nuclear waste from France docked safely in northern Japan on Tuesday.

Escorted by two tug boats and six police helicopters flying overhead, the Pacific Teal ended an eight-week trip from the French port of Cherbourg that took it past about 20 nations which had protested at it passing near their shores.

The ship's arrival at the port of Mutsu-Ogawara comes amid a rise in anti-nuclear sentiment in Japan after a radiation leak from a nuclear fuel reprocessing plant last week that ranks as Japan's worst nuclear accident.
The accident exposed 37 workers to radiation and revealed major safety flaws in the country's nuclear power industry.
Under the terms of an agreement between Japan, Britain and France, spent Japanese uranium fuel is reprocessed overseas into plutonium and the waste is returned to Japan for storage.

About 150 activists from environmental groups such as Greenpeace lined a road outside the harbour complex within sight of the ship to protest against its cargo, which included radioactive material such as strontium.

But the protests were minor compared with demonstrations over the first waste shipment which arrived in April 1995 at this port about 580 km (360 miles) northeast of Tokyo, which was custom-built to handle nuclear waste shipments.
Police linked hands to form a human cordon in case there was any surge towards the wharf by the protesters.
But the protesters confined themselves to holding aloft anti-nuclear banners and singing songs denouncing nuclear power as a threat to the environment.
The waste on the ship will be mixed with glass and encased in 40 stainless steel canisters.

After tests for any leakage of radiation, the canisters will be stored for 30 to 50 years at a special cooling facility at nearby Rokkasho village, Japan's only such storage place, and later buried at an unspecified location.
The government has not selected the ultimate destination and residents fear they may be stuck with the toxic material.
Greenpeace Japan spokeswoman Noriko Oyama told reporters the tide was turning against nuclear power, which meets about one-third of energy-poor Japan's electricity needs.

The controversy over Japan's reliance on nuclear power intensified after the March 11 radiation leak caused by a fire and explosion at the Tokaimura nuclear processing plant 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo.

An investigation of the accident has so far revealed startling lapses in safety standards, including outdated firefighting equipment and delays in alerting both local residents and central authorities of the crisis.
Since the Tokaimura incident, two other nuclear reactors, part of a 50-reactor network, have either shut or cut back production because of flaws in their operations.
Tokyo plans eventually to ship 7,100 tonnes of spent fuel to France and Britain for reprocessing into 30 tonnes of fuel-grade plutonium, yielding 3,000 tonnes of waste.
Japan plans to move to plutonium technology to boost its energy self-sufficiency rate to more than 50 percent by early next century.
